title: The Jewel Mirror Samadhi
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk explores the concept of true mirror samadhi, or the ultimate reality that lies beyond concepts and dualities, as described by Dongshan Liangzhe's poem on the five ranks of enlightenment. This idea emphasizes a progression from recognizing one's personal nature within the universal to achieving unity and freedom, but also highlights the importance of humility and connection with others. By letting go of fixed notions of spiritual stages or ranks, practitioners can instead cultivate mindfulness and turn towards difficult emotions and thoughts with gentleness, leading to greater compassion and non-judgmental awareness.

sentences.text: **Kanho Chris Burkhart:** Can you hear me now?
Good morning.
I apologize for my internet dropping out, so it might happen again.
I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.
Good morning and welcome to our October event in our Zen Alive series.
I also have some good news about Zen Alive, just in case you have not heard.
It will continue on a weekly basis in 2021 with your support.
The general theme of the coming year will be conversations around awakening, practice enlightenment, or as Dogen Zenji calls it, ji jiu yu sun mai, self-fulfilling samadhi, or practice enlightenment.
I'm very much looking forward to a deeper exploration of that.
However, since we're still in 2020, we continue to study our Zen chants with an eye toward the question how we can understand what the chants say in our everyday life.
If you have not encountered the true mirror samadhi before, you will probably find it pretty confusing, as I did and still do.
However, I was fortunate enough to spend a practice period at Green Gorge studying the true mirror samadhi under Abbot Steve Stuckey, who was an excellent teacher.
I remember that I was really stuck on the lines: Yi, with his archer skill, could hit a target at 100 paces.
But when arrow points meet head on, what does this have to do with the power of skill?
So I brought up this question in Dokusan, and that I just simply could not get it.
Abbot Steve smiled and then started to laugh.
Zen was easy.
And he said that we don't reach an understanding in Zen because you read a certain number of books, or because you do so and so many practice periods.
But that those things certainly help.
And arrow points meeting in midair are not brought about by skill.
Abbot Steve was a tall big man with a big laugh.
Today, I would add, if Yi had not ever touched bow and arrow, it would have been unlikely that arrow points meet midair.
So what does the true mirror samadhi say?
Dongshan, who wrote the true mirror samadhi, they say, says that the world, the universe is made out of two elements, sameness and difference.
That speech may be treacherous and that the relative and absolute are one.
The true mirror samadhi says that in no thought, in absence of discrimination lies liberation.
And it also says that all things are in relationship.
This poem, the true mirror, appears in our Zen literature under different names.
In the Avatamsaka Sutra, it is the true Dharma realm.
In the Lotus Sutra, our one true nature.
In the mind only school, it is the Alaya Vishnana, which is the result of transformation of the ordinary consciousness.
So today we take a closer look at the true mirror samadhi.
It is often attributed to Dongshan, also called Tungshan Liangzhe.
In Japan, he was known as Tosan Ryokai.
He lived from 807 to 869.
And together with Sao Chan Benji, he was one of the founders of the Saodong school.
So Sao comes from Sao Chan and Dong from Dongshan, Saodong school.
And it was one of the five houses of Zen in China.
Of course, Dogen Zenji's teacher in China was an eminent teacher of the Chinese Saodong lineage.
As I mentioned, the true mirror samadhi was only attributed to Dongshan.
Its authorship is not quite certain.
Some scholars think that one of Dongshan's spiritual ancestors might have written it.
The poem was first mentioned in Xue Fan, Wei Hong's biographical compilation of 1119.

And I thought it was a bit funny when I read in one of the commentaries that Dongshan could not have written the true mirror samadhi because the other things he had written were way too brilliant for him to have written the true mirror samadhi.
But for the sake of this talk, let us assume that Dongshan wrote the poem.
So once we start to unravel the code words and phrases in this poem and relate them to other Zen stories, the poem becomes more and more expansive.
In this talk, I will only touch on two of the code phrases, with emphasis on the last one.
The first thing I would like to talk about is the opening of the poem.
And the second thing is what is known as Dongshan's Five Ranks.
And I should add that this is my current understanding of the Five Ranks.
It goes much deeper than what I can talk about at this time and what I understand at this time.
But it's truly fascinating.
So let us start at the beginning.
*The teaching of dasanas has been intimately communicated by Buddhas and ancestors.
Now you have it, so keep it well.*
Let me repeat that.
*The teaching of dasanas has been intimately communicated by Buddhas and ancestors.
Now you have it, so keep it well.*
You may be familiar with case one from the Book of Serenity, which points at the same in different words.
*One day, the World Honored One ascended the seat.
Manjushri struck the gavel and said, "Clearly observe the Dharma of the King of Dharma.
The Dharma of the King of Dharma is thus."
The World Honored One then got down from the seat.*
In the Mahayana tradition, dasanas is a central notion.
It refers to the Absolute, to reality, the true nature of all things, formless, unmade, devoid of self-nature, immovable, beyond concepts.
Dasanas or suchness is the opposite of that which is apparent, while at the same time it does absolutely include the apparent.
It includes all phenomena.
Nothing is left out.
It is present right now.
It says, "Now you have it, so keep it well."
It says that because you have always had it, you have never been apart from it, not for a single moment.
However, it is possible that vexations cover up our Buddha nature quite thoroughly. [unclear: "I am enlightened.
I am not enlightened by just expressions."] The mirror is always there, unchanged and unchanging, however our mental games prevent that reflection.
Dogen wrote a wonderful fascicle called Old Mirror, and it's called Old Mirror in the Tanahashi translation of the Shobo Genso.
It would be tempting to read the whole essay, however I will limit it to two brief sections.
And if you have the Shobo Genso, it is on page 207 and 209 what I'm going to read.
So Dogen writes:
*The great round mirror is the power of all Buddhas.
There is no obscuration inside or out, means that there is no inside other than outside, and no outside that has any obscuration inside.
This mirror has no front or back.
As for two people have one understanding and their minds and eyes are alike, being alike means that one person meets another.
The image inside has mind, eye, and one understanding.
The reflection outside has mind, eye, and one understanding.
The bodies, minds, and environs of the two people that emerge are alike inside and outside.*
*There is neither self nor other.
Two people encounter, two people are alike.
Other is called self, self becomes other.
Mind and eyes alike means the minds are like the minds, the eyes are like the eyes.
Being alike is minds and eyes.
It is just like saying that both minds and eyes are alike.
Minds are alike just as the third ancestor or the sixth ancestor.
Eye and eye are alike just as the eye of the way is immersed in the eye.*
Now I'm switching to the next segment.
*Xue Feng, great master Chen Chao, once taught the assembly, "If you want to understand the essential matter, it is like an old mirror I have in myself.
When a barbarian comes, a barbarian appears.
When a Chinese person comes, a Chinese person appears."
Xuan Cha came out and said, "What about the moment when you encounter the emergence of a bright mirror all of a sudden?"
Xue Feng said, "Both the barbarian and the Chinese person disappear."
Xuan Cha said, "I have a different understanding."
Xue Feng said, "How do you understand?"
Xuan Cha said, "Please ask me a question."
Xue Feng said, "What about the moment when you encounter the emergence of a bright mirror all of a sudden?"
Xuan Cha said, "100 broken pieces."
For the moment, investigate the essential matter spoken of by Xue Feng.
What is it?
For the moment, take a look at Xue Feng's old mirror.
The words like an old mirror I have in myself mean that the mirror is completely boundless and not limited by outside or inside.
It is a pearl rolling on a board.*
So I'm sure that in these lines, you saw some pieces of the true mirror samadhi looking back at you.
Last but not least, the true mirror samadhi is about Dongshan's Five Ranks.
In the past, the true mirror samadhi and the Five Ranks have been a tool to evaluate or to look at the practice of a Zen student.
I do not believe that this practice is still common today.
I have not heard of it.
So if you read through the poem, you see several references to the number five.
Some of them are obvious.
Some of them are kind of hidden, like the diamond thunderbolt.
And if you enjoy the I Ching, you might really enjoy reading up on the Five Ranks because they can also be expressed that way.
I myself, I'm ignorant about the I Ching.
So all I can do is refer you to Shen Yan's book, The Infinite Mirror, which goes on quite a bit about that.
So the first three degrees are based more on intellect and the last two express action or effort.
Actually, the third step is kind of a pivot point.
It is a transition at which it goes from intellect into life.
The world of phenomena is dominant, but it is already seen as a dimension of the absolute self.
I would like to read a poem that Dongshan wrote about it.
And it has five stanzas.
And it starts with the apparent within the real.
*The apparent within the real, in the third watch of the night before the moon appears.
No wonder when we meet, there is no recognition.
Still cherished in my heart is the beauty of earlier days.*
So now we move to the second stanza.
The undifferentiated aspect comes forth, and diversity recedes a bit into the background.
This stanza is usually called the real within the apparent.
*A sleepy-eyed grandam encounters herself in the mirror.
Clearly she sees a face.
But it doesn't resemble hers at all.
Too bad, with a muddled head, she tried to recognize her reflection.*
At the third level, no awareness of body or mind remain.
Both drop away completely.
Dongshan's third stanza is usually called the coming from within the real.
*The coming from within the real.
Within nothingness, there is a path leading away from the dust of the world.
Even if you observe the taboo on the present emperor's name, you will surpass that eloquent one of yours who silenced every tongue.*
So, the fourth stanza.
The level of attainment.
In this level of attainment, the singularity of each object is perceived.
And one recognizes how unique each and everything is.
The difference between this level and the next is not very great.
And through understanding how unique everything is, one also sees how everything is connected. [unclear: "Bumblebee, go away."] This stanza is called the arrival at mutual integration.
*The arrival at mutual integration.
When two blades cross points, there is no need to withdraw.
The master swordsman is like the lotus blooming in the fire.
Such a man has in and of himself a heaven-soaring spirit.*
At this, the fifth and highest level is brought forth by Dongshan.
Form and emptiness mutually penetrate to such a degree that there is no longer any consciousness of either.
Ideas of enlightenment and illusion vanish.
It is a stage of perfect inner freedom and is referred to as unity attained.
*Unity attained.
Who dares to equal him who falls into neither being or non-being?
All men want to leave the current of ordinary life, but he, after all, comes back to sit among the coal and ashes.*
So what did we just listen to?
I am going to give a slightly different summary.
Stanza one, the personal within the universal.
At this level, once original nature starts to come forth, the possibility of a different way of living in the world is seen.
Grounded in experiential certainty, observation, and inquiry.
The second stanza, the universal within the personal.
The universal is the dominant sphere acting as a container for the thoughts, feelings, and aspirations of the personal.
Stanza three, coming from within the universal.
The inconceivable mind comes to the forefront.
A world where the personal and universal are united.
Four, arriving within the personal.
Within this rank, the universal and personal beneficially interact, refining the attributes of the personal.
I believe this is exactly what people usually understand as utter enlightenment.
But then there is level five, attainment in both the personal and universal, so that they respond in harmony to each other and the world at large.
And you might ask, why is not enlightenment the highest stage?
Why, why, why is it basically based in delusion again?
And what I understand from what I have read is that the person of absolute enlightenment does not see any difference between self and other any longer.
And how can we step forward and help?
How can we be helpful and useful to the humans around us and the world if we cannot tell the difference anymore?
This is the end of my talk.
I hope it has been helpful.
If all I have done is so in confusion, please forget every word I said and just go on with your day.
Thank you so very much.
May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
*Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to end them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
Thank you very much.
Could we unmute and have a conversation about it?
I don't know if I can answer any questions, but I am curious what people got from this.
**Participant:** I wonder if you could, if you have any examples from your life where some of these ideas from the five ranks have popped in or been helpful.
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** I see how I personally have changed through practice.
I've been at it for about two decades and I see how definitely the shift from no training at all to the first rank, which is life goes on pretty much as it did.
But there starts to be a grounding in practice, in the precepts, in the paramitas.
So the everyday actions become more grounded in Buddhist teaching.
And then a shift to the second stage, and I find one of the books really helpful, the way they laid it out.
The infinite mirror.
And the visualization in that is really neat.
So he says we start out.
Can everybody see that?
He has basically a black circle with a little bit of white at the bottom and the white basically represents the grounding in Buddha Dharma.

And then he goes to the second level, which is basically your life is grounded in Buddha Dharma, but old habit energies, conditioning behaviors, often unknown conditioning, unexamined beliefs still remain.
I think this one is really cute.
It's kind of like our hindrances and vexations are surrounded by Buddha nature and Buddha Dharma.
And then this is what, when I started to practice, this is what I definitely wanted to reach, this enlightenment.

And it was the promise of a totally different worldview, just to understand, truly understand that when you touch this for a second, day or life, one needs to come back to be utterly immersed in our vexations.
Our hindrances are the path.
We cannot ever get to this without that.
And this is what we need to return to.
I don't know if this was just a recap of the talk.
**Participant:** That was really helpful.
Thanks, Chris.
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** Yeah, it's nice little symbols.
And I posted one of the ways that the five ranks are titled into the chat too.
**Participant:** Oh, wonderful.
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** And for people who really are interested in the I Ching, this is how it relates.
Yeah, and it's in this book.
**Participant:** Chris, can anybody hear me?
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** Yes.
**Participant:** I just had a comment that it all feels very similar to the, you know, the ox herding.
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** Exactly.

**Participant:** Where, you know, you start out, you know, you enter the, you know, some understanding and then when you enter full understanding, you know, the last step is always returned to the marketplace, returned to the world that we live in, you know, to be there.

It's kind of like also Dogen's thing with, I think, you know, about the mountains, you know, are just mountains, but then you go through and mountains are no longer mountains and then, you know, mountains are mountains.
They're different, but they're the same.
So that was the feeling I had with the five stages.
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** That is wonderful because the ox herding pictures are often referenced as an equivalent to understanding.

**Participant:** You know, Chris, in my life, what the thing that I kind of, when I hear the five ranks, I kind of go, whoa, I mean that, you know, the different levels, and it implies that there's this stage, then there's this stage.
In my life personally, you know, I may have a day or a moment of clarity but then in the next moment I'm just as confused as I was before, you know, I think you say over the years.

I mean, you hardly, in my experience, you know, you don't notice, maybe, I mean I noticed that back and forth, but it just kind of things tend to mellow over the years in that way, but I feel like sometimes when I read these things you know about this kind of developmental approach, stage by stage, it makes me feel, I don't know what the word is, but maybe that's not quite reality, at least to go so stepwise.
And of course we talk about no attainment.
So when I read that stuff, it puts this pressure on me, like, I'm really behind here or something.
That's how I experience it in my everyday world.
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** Thank you, Kate.
I totally hear you.
One thing I should say: I really, really, really simplified that teaching.
And like all the Zen things, it's not A or B.
It's not either/or.
In one spot it says that each and every one of the ranks includes all the other, all of them.
It's like the parameters.
It's not that there is dana parameter and it's totally disconnected from the other five, or that wisdom is disconnected from dana or energy or ethical conduct.
It's one ball of wax, but every once in a while we point out and mold a certain part of it to be a little more prominent in a conversation.
So all of these things are to be taken with a grain of salt, absolutely.
And like everything in Zen, the five ranks are not a five-step program.
They are wild.
You can be in one and pop into four with no thought, or someone who has never practiced can walk down the street and have an enlightenment experience.
It's deeply disturbing if that happens to them, but it does happen.
So it's a tool to look at how my practice is, and what direction my practice is moving.
It's not a dogma.
It's something to help lightly, but something really interesting, I think.
And by the way, if you ever get really nerdy and you want to go into the five ranks, Sheng Yen is really awesome.
It's a very, very readable commentary.
And then Ross Bolleter has a very scholarly book on the five ranks.
And the translation of the five stanzas that I used is the one from Thomas Cleary.
It doesn't seem to be something we actually study a lot in our tradition.
We don't bring it up that much.
And Dongshan was really, really important for our school, because Soto Zen grew out of the Sao Dong school in China.
The Japanese version of Sao Dong was a [unclear: "dogma named print"].
Soto is literally the Japanese voicing of those two characters, so it's literally the same.
**Participant:** Thank you.
Yeah, and Changyan is a good person to know about.
He's a modern Taiwanese teacher and started a huge Dharma organization called Dharma Drum.
There's a monastery of his in Richmond, outside of Vancouver.
He's since passed on.
He's a very accessible traditional teacher, one of those people who does a good job bridging between Asia and the West.

I like expanding our focus a little bit with some of the ancient teachers and bringing different pieces together, so that we aren't all totally focused too tightly on one teacher, one tradition or whatever.
I like that, so I appreciate it when we bring up some other people that aren't necessarily in our immediate study all the time.
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** Yeah, way to go for it, Chris.
Also, if you want to totally geek out on the Jewel Mirror Samadhi, comb through the internet and find Charlie Pokorny's commentary on it.
He analyzed each Chinese character and the different meanings of the words.
It's kind of interesting but super dense.

So I'd like to hear some other questions still, because I'm a little bit worried that this was too far outside of what we usually talk about, and I would really like to know if this was useful beyond the intellectual engagement with something new and tasty.
**Participant:** Something I know sometimes in these tiered teachings is that it can be useful as a mindfulness practice of recognizing what mind state I happen to be in in the moment.
So I wondered, do you have any advice on how to recognize which of those ranks we happen to be in in a given moment?
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** I would really suggest not getting too stuck on saying, oh, am I one, two, three, four, five?
That is not useful, because that drags the whole thing into the intellectual realm: oh, I must be doing quite badly because right now I'm totally stuck in one, and usually I'm a number four.
It's more like a general feeling that you might have for your practice in general.
So please do not use this to diminish your practice.
Don't use the mirror to be critical of yourself.
Please go ahead.

**Participant:** I mean, not necessarily from a critical viewpoint, but sometimes I find it alleviating to my inner critic voice to recognize, oh, right now I'm feeling very thought-prompt and I'm feeling anxious and I'm in a mind state that's not very spacious.
Sometimes I find that really liberating, to notice that and not judge myself for it.
And to be able to recognize, oh, right now I'm feeling less thought-prompt.
One of my favorite texts from the Pali Canon is the Satipatthana Sutta.
That's the thing he talks about there: recognizing what our mind state is in a non-judgmental way, just being mindful.
What is the nature of my mind at a given moment?
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** Great.
So I would answer that from my point of view at this time, which might change in the future: I would not use the five ranks for that at all.
The five ranks are more of a big-picture thing.
If you feel anxious, if you feel perturbed, and by gosh, we've got plenty of reason right now to have this anxiety, right?
There's so much going on in the news and not much of it is good.
So I suggest going back to the very foundational practice, which is to sit with it and see what comes up around it.
And when you identify one of the core issues for you, so this is what is really disturbing me, the uncertainty or fear, whatever, turn towards it.
Our practice is always to turn toward that which is difficult, that which is hard, to become intimate with the things we really don't like.
And that is a great way of disarming them.
You might make peace with something and five minutes later it's back again with the next newsflash or the next thought, whatever.
And then again the gentle turning towards it.
It's a gentle turning towards it.
It's not grabbing it by the throat and shaking it till it gives up.
But what is it that I'm afraid of?
I deal with fears around the political system right now.
And it's just always: what am I afraid of?
And how am I right now?
Because fear is always about something in the future.
I heard Jack Kornfield once tell this great story.
He says, you're out hiking in the north and you see these huge paw prints that can only belong to a grizzly.
You get really worried.
But think about it: there are the paw prints, they don't hurt you, nothing is happening.
You just wonder where that critter is that left these huge paw prints.
And that's what we are afraid of, the future.
And then you turn around the corner and what do you see?
The owner of the paw prints, right?
There is a big grizzly.
And then the heart really starts going.
What am I afraid of?
Well, you look at the grizzly, and you're basically fine.
The grizzly is over there.
But you're really afraid of what is going to happen next.
And then the grizzly starts charging you.
You're still fine, but you're really worried about what happens when your body and the grizzly meet.
And then the grizzly attacks you and bites you, and that's pain.
But that's still not fear.
The fear is: is that grizzly going to stop?
Where is it going to stop?
So the fear is always about something in the future.
That was something that really helped me in my practice, to identify that fear is projecting into the future, and it's my thoughts.
I don't know if that was helpful at all.
**Participant:** You know, Chris, I got to tell you, I had an experience in the wilderness encountering a grizzly.
This bear was probably how many feet away?
I don't know, less than 10 feet away from me.
And you don't think.
In the moment, both of us looked at each other, we looked at each other in the eyes, and we both simultaneously, very carefully, just walked away from each other.
Afterwards I thought, oh, my God.
But it's like that, because it isn't fear in the moment.
You're just your body.
Just in that instance, it did the right thing.
So I know what you're saying there with all that.
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** That's a great story, and it makes much more sense than what I did when a black bear almost walked over me.
My partner Reg and I were sleeping at a riverbank, just sleeping bags, no tent.
And he knocks on my shoulder and he goes, look, look, black bear.
And there was this black bear literally shambling along the riverbank, just walking towards us.
Their eyesight is terrible, and the wind was coming from his direction.
And I'm going, oh, that's great.
And then Reg's throwing some rocks at it so he wouldn't stumble into us.
So, well, friends, any last thoughts?
**Participant:** Yeah, Corinne had something.
I just wanted to ask: when you're turning towards those emotions, what does that intimacy look like?
Because sometimes when I'm turning towards those emotions, it ratchets it up.
So how does that intimacy help you to become friends with it?
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** Let's just use one example: political figures I don't like.
I feel extremely strongly about that.

I think my German background really has me shy away from anything that smells of dictatorship, and of trying to limit people, trying to make people other so you can ostracize them and make them the enemy.
I'm reacting super strongly to that, and that's what's been going on for the last four years: making people other.
So one thing that is always helpful is to find the part inside myself that does that, that makes someone other or different.
So let's use political views.
I find where inside me is this part that wants to say, I don't want to have anything to do with these people because they are so different.
And we encounter acquaintances, neighbors whose views are extremely different, and we might not choose to hang out with them because they are so different.
So I identify the part in me that also holds those views, about a different subject, probably.
And then I spend time with that feeling.
And I come to see that just like I'm afraid of people who make people of color other, I might treat a person who leans towards these extreme views as other.
I don't want to be anything like him.
I don't want that person in my life.
I don't want to deal with that person.
It was a shock for me when I read the study that in 2016 many Republicans were as afraid of four more years of Obama-like as I was afraid of four years of Trump.
So they are just like us, just like me.
They just have a different foundational thinking.
And when I come to that point, I realize, yeah.
And then, for example, when I look at the geographic distribution of politics, if you look at the American Heartland, it's solid red.
So basically, if you're born in a certain area code, that will in part determine what your views are.
So it cannot be just myself or them.
It's the environment.
It's the upbringing.
It's the ethics that they were brought up with.
It's very hard to put into words, but it's not affirming that they are different or bad.
It's affirming our saneness.
And yes, I will still totally donate to the political party that I prefer and support people that I'm more aligned with.
Just because I'm getting over the spiteful thinking doesn't mean I support that person in the outcome.
I've been doing meditation for Donald Trump for a long time.
I failed.
Okay, so it doesn't always work.

**Participant:** I'd maybe add that these teachings on the absolute and emptiness all sound very abstract, but actually they're practical in these kinds of areas, too.

I think Dongshan's Five Ranks are very practical in that way, actually.
I don't think it's just an abstract, weird-ass teaching.

He's talking about lots of fluid perspectives, like Chris was just talking about with that example of politics.

What will be the next thing?
That was his question, I guess.
Well, then what?
Well, then what?
Well, then what?
So it's like the sense of a journey of understanding.
